narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in the third year of law school had the strongest influence. Being in the fifth decile placed you slightly below the average of students who were admitted, and this pulled the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 30.5 was the second most important factor. It sits noticeably below the 37.2 average of accepted students and therefore pushed the outcome toward failing the bar. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 was the third key driver; falling short of the 3.23 average among accepted applicants also nudged the prediction in the direction of failure.

Although your upper-middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the decision, the combination of these academic signals led the model to conclude your risk of not passing the bar was too high for admission.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, improving your academic performance in later law school years, or considering schools with different admissions thresholds would be the most direct next steps.
